clue.text: Fix cricket? Its body has virtually no substance

definitions.text: Its body has virtually no substance

parts.note: to fix something in place is to stick it
a cricket is one kind of insect

explanation.surface: A question about rigging a cricket match, then a remark that something's frame is flimsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cricket' looks like the sport after 'Fix' (as in match-fixing), but it is the chirping creature, an example of an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: This creature is famously twig-thin, a body of almost no bulk at all.

clue.text: Very large rubbish brought up in trunk

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing something up turns it upside down, so these letters are read bottom to top

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
rot is nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: Someone finds an enormous load of junk hauled up inside a travelling chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' turns the whole run OSROT, reading it bottom to top in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The trunk is the main body of a person, excluding head and limbs.

clue.text: One Catholic in event remains

indicators.note: the pair of pieces sits in the middle of the word for event, enclosed by it

parts.note: a case is an instance or event, as in 'in the event'
A is one, as in 'a pound'
RC is the usual abbreviation for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: A lone Catholic attends some occasion where human remains are involved.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead body, especially an animal's, is what is left: the remains.

clue.text: Drill at home silent mostly

parts.note: being in means being at home

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word but not all, so the final letter goes

parts.note: still means quiet or silent
the last letter of the word for silent

explanation.surface: Advice on keeping quiet while practising a drill indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: To drill a lesson into someone is to impress it on them gradually by repetition.

clue.text: Back set for surgery that's most serious

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship

indicators.note: something sent for surgery gets cut up and rearranged, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A patient's back is booked in for an operation at its gravest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like part of the body in surgery, but it is the rear of a ship; 'for surgery' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Stern means grave or severe, so the superlative is the gravest of all.

clue.text: Fool daily with story

parts.note: a daily, or char, is a British term for a cleaning lady who comes in daily
a story is a fib or lie

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor dismisses a daily paper and its tale as foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' suggests a newspaper, but here it is the old British word for a cleaner, a charwoman or char.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlie is British slang for a silly person or idiot.

clue.text: Maverick had lovely idea to get really rich

indicators.note: a maverick goes its own unorthodox way, so these letters are put in an unconventional order

explanation.surface: A maverick entrepreneur comes up with a great idea and makes a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maverick' reads like a noun for a person, but it signals the anagram of HAD LOVELY IDEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaded is slang for having plenty of money; with the intensifier it means extremely wealthy.

clue.text: Crack and ecstasy with time can bring on madness

indicators.note: to crack something is to break it into pieces, so the letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A warning that crack cocaine and ecstasy, taken over time, can lead to insanity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' and 'ecstasy' read as a pair of drugs, but 'Crack' is the anagram signal for AND, E and TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a decline in mental faculties, an old sense being insanity.

clue.text: Wearing unorthodox clothing, angry dash to mayo?

parts.note: cross means annoyed or angry
mayo, short for mayonnaise, is a salad dressing

explanation.surface: Someone angrily slaps mayonnaise on, oddly dressed while doing so.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a cross dash of mayonnaise on a salad; the pieces are cross (angry) plus dressing (mayo).
explanation.definitionFit: This means dressing in clothes usually worn by the opposite sex.

clue.text: Slip made by rascal losing his head

indicators.note: losing a head means the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a terror is a mischievous child or rascal
the first letter of the word for rascal

explanation.surface: A mistake made by a scoundrel who has been beheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip is a small mistake or blunder.

clue.text: Cut outside engagement and cry

indicators.note: the word for cut goes outside, enclosing the word for engagement

parts.note: to shear is to cut
a date is a social engagement or appointment

explanation.surface: Someone cancels an engagement and weeps.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase means to weep, to let fall a drop from the eye.

clue.text: Instrument manoeuvred into breach

parts.note: a viola is a stringed instrument

indicators.note: manoeuvred means moved around, so these letters are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: A musical instrument is steered through a gap in a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manoeuvred' rearranges the word after it; 'breach' looks like a gap in a wall but means an infringement of a rule.
explanation.definitionFit: A breach of a rule or law is an infringement of it.

clue.text: Directions announced for a city

indicators.note: announced means spoken out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: leads are directions or guidance, as in leads given to detectives

explanation.surface: Someone calls out the route to a city.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds is a large city in Yorkshire, northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a city in West Yorkshire, England.

clue.text: Steps out of bed very drunk

indicators.note: the letters of the word bed are taken out of the longer word, wherever they fall

parts.note: bladdered is British slang for very drunk
the word bed is taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles out of bed after a heavy night, completely intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: BLADDERED is British slang for very drunk; 'out of' removes B, E and D (the first letter and the last two), leaving the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladder is a set of steps for climbing.

clue.text: Hector after operation: I'm doreen!

indicators.note: after an operation a patient has been rearranged by surgery, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A patient named Doreen, after surgery, speaks; Hector is the name of a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hector' looks like a man's name, but it is a verb meaning to bully.
explanation.definitionFit: To hector is to bully or browbeat someone, to boss them about.

clue.text: In ecstasy about Sade novel? The opposite agreed

indicators.note: about would put one word round the other, enclosing it
the opposite reverses the order just stated, so the outer and inner words swap roles
novel means new, so these letters are made new by rearrangement

parts.note: sent is an old slang word meaning thrilled or in ecstasy

explanation.surface: A reader is thrilled by a novel by de Sade, or perhaps the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' alone would put the ecstasy word round the jumbled name; 'The opposite' flips that, so the anagram (signalled by 'novel') goes round the outside instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To assent is to agree to something, so this is the past tense of consenting.

clue.text: Listed computer stuff is to be kept in eastern Mediterranean

parts.note: IT stands for information technology, computer stuff

indicators.note: the word is goes inside the next pieces, kept within them

explanation.surface: Computer equipment is listed as being stored somewhere in the eastern Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: To itemise is to list things one by one, so this is the past tense.

clue.text: Alternatively it's "beat" and "slam"

indicators.note: alternatively suggests another arrangement, so these letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A remark that a word can mean both to thrash and to criticise harshly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the wordplay, an anagram of BEAT and SLAM, and also the definition, since the answer means both beat and slam.
explanation.definitionFit: To lambaste is to thrash physically or to criticise harshly.

clue.text: Suet rolls inside are not of luxury type

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go inside the word are
rolls means turns over, so these letters are tumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Suet rolls are plain, homely food, not luxurious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rolls' looks like a noun (suet pudding rolls) but is the verb signalling the anagram, and 'inside' puts the result within the clue word are.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere means plain, without comfort or adornment.

clue.text: Attack flipping boring, old men on English

indicators.note: on means following, so the abbreviation comes after
flipping means turning over, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: old farts is a slang term for boring old men

explanation.surface: Someone launches a tirade about tedious old men attacking the English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' reads like a mild British swear word but signals the reversal; old farts is slang for dull old men, and 'on' puts the English letter after.
explanation.definitionFit: To strafe is to attack with gunfire from low-flying aircraft.

clue.text: Name given to fat said to cause upset

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the pieces are taken by their sound

parts.note: a term is a name, and oil is a fat in the cooking sense, so a name given to fat is a term for oil

explanation.surface: A complaint that the label on some fat is causing distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given to' joins the two pieces, term (name) and oil (fat); 'said' means the pair is heard, not spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Turmoil is a state of disturbance, confusion or upset.

clue.text: Screen in place, a mini with no lines showing

parts.note: PL is the abbreviation for place, as in street names

indicators.note: with no means without, so the named letters are removed

parts.note: mini means small
L is short for line, so two lines are LL

explanation.surface: A screen fitted in a Mini car with no visible lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mini' suggests the car, but it is just the adjective small; removing LL (lines) leaves SMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A plasma is a type of flat television screen.

clue.text: Leaving tiger's head, jeers for some wedding guests?

indicators.note: leaving means going away, so the named letter is taken out

parts.note: taunts are jeers or insults

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A tiger's head is left behind as guests jeer at a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: A father's or mother's sisters are typical relatives invited to a marriage.

clue.text: Thousand sick with runs in water channels

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
ill means sick
races are runs, as in sprinting

explanation.surface: A thousand people fall ill after running races in canals.
explanation.definitionFit: A millrace is the channel carrying water to turn a mill wheel.

clue.text: American Indian not OK in fabric

indicators.note: not means without, so the two letters are removed

parts.note: the Chinook are a Native American people of the Pacific Northwest
OK is taken as written

explanation.surface: An American Indian is unhappy with some fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Chino is a strong cotton twill fabric used for trousers.

clue.text: Early drink for soccer teams?

parts.note: football sides have eleven players each, so plural elevens become a mid-morning break; the cryptic reading makes the British snack time sound like squads

explanation.surface: Football squads stop for a morning cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a British mid-morning snack or drink, taken around eleven o'clock; a soccer team is an eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: This British term names a light mid-morning refreshment, such as tea and biscuits.

clue.text: One's squeezed between two legs? It's enough to make one 11

indicators.note: the single letter is squeezed between the two copies of the word
two means the word for legs is used twice

parts.note: on is the leg side in cricket
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Something is squashed between a pair of legs, enough to bring tears.
explanation.walkthrough: ON is the leg side in cricket; 11 refers to the answer to 11-across, to cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Chopping this vegetable releases fumes that make people weep.

clue.text: First dance with nothing on shouldn't go down like this

parts.note: to lead is to be first
a ball is a formal dance
O looks like zero, nothing
on is taken as written

explanation.surface: A first dance done naked shouldn't be a flop.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'go down like a lead balloon' means to be received badly and fail.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy metal balloon would sink, so the idiom describes something that fails to impress.
